raw_task:
Stress-test this 4-layer database architecture for a Finnish hospitality holding (10 companies, ~50 staff). We build AI features on top of these databases — the goal is compound interest: each feature added makes the whole system smarter.

THE 4 LAYERS:
1. KNOWLEDGE LAYER: Obsidian vault (Markdown + YAML frontmatter). Obsidian Bases = SQLite auto-generated from frontmatter. Stores: customer context, interaction history, SOPs, kanban views, chatbot content (tier-4). Write: Patrick + auto-gen scripts only. Agents never write directly to vault.
2. STRUCTURED LAYER: Excel MVP → Supabase (PostgreSQL, EU Frankfurt). Tables: customers, contacts, bookings, interactions, scores, agent_logs. One Supabase project, RLS per company_id.
3. ANALYTICS LAYER: Power BI on top of Excel/Supabase. Embedded as iframes in FinnConcierge staff app.
4. VERSION/AUDIT LAYER: Git. All code, prompts, n8n workflow JSON versioned here.

FEATURES AND HOW THEY USE THE LAYERS:
- @scorer: reads K2 (structured scores) → writes K1 (today.md) + triggers K3 (Power BI refresh)
- Second Brain: reads+writes K1 (interaction .md) AND K2 (interactions table) — needs BOTH
- @chatbot: reads K1 tier-4 MD (pre-ingested into K2 SQLite/Supabase index)
- Email Drafter: reads K1 (customer notes/context) + K2 (deal history structure)
- FinnConcierge: reads/writes K2, shows K3 embedded

CHALLENGE THESE 4 THINGS:
1. Is K1 (Obsidian MD) a real database or a liability? When does markdown-as-database break? What's the failure mode when 10 companies × 200 customers = 2000 MD files?
2. K1+K2 dual-write risk: Second Brain and Email Drafter need BOTH Obsidian and Supabase. What happens when they drift out of sync? Which is source of truth?
3. Single Supabase project with RLS per company_id — safe for 10 companies with different data sensitivity? Or should each company have its own Supabase project?
4. Is this architecture truly compound-interest (each feature makes next feature cheaper/better) or is it actually 4 separate systems that create maintenance overhead?

Be specific. Name failure modes. GO/CONDITIONAL GO/NO GO per layer. 8/10 verbosity.
response:
Thought for 40s

Overall stress-test verdict: This 4-layer architecture is solid and forward-looking for a 10-company Finnish hospitality holding (~50 staff, ~2000 customers). It cleverly hybridizes human-centric knowledge (Obsidian) with production-grade ops (Supabase) and analytics (Power BI), while Git provides the audit backbone. The “compound interest” goal works because the layers are intentionally leaky in a controlled way: rich Markdown context from K1 makes AI features (scorer, chatbot, drafter) dramatically smarter without duplicating effort. At this scale it holds up well, but it has clear brittle edges around synchronization, schema discipline, and RLS policy hygiene. Below I tackle your four challenges head-on with named failure modes, real-world scalability data, and per-layer GO/CONDITIONAL GO/NO GO.

1. Is K1 (Obsidian MD + YAML + Obsidian Bases SQLite) a real database or a liability? When does markdown-as-database break? Failure modes at 10×200 = 2000 MD files?

It is a hybrid knowledge database, not a pure production one — and at 2000 files it is still a strength, not a liability. Obsidian + Bases (core plugin) auto-generates SQLite views from frontmatter, giving you Dataview-style tables, kanbans, and graph queries on customer context, SOPs, tier-4 chatbot content, etc. Real users run 15 000-note vaults “extremely fast” on SSDs; official stress tests and forum reports show 10k–50k notes remain responsive. 2000 customer files + SOPs/kanbans = well under the pain threshold.⁠Reddit +1

Markdown-as-database breaks when you need:

True ACID transactions / concurrent writes (Obsidian has none; file-system writes can corrupt on crash).
Enforced schema (YAML is free-form; one missing company_id or typo in last_interaction breaks Bases tables).
Complex relational joins or millisecond analytics (Dataview/Bases are good but slower than native Postgres for 10-table queries).
High-frequency writes by agents (explicitly forbidden here — good).

Specific failure modes at your scale:

Frontmatter drift / parse errors: Auto-gen SQLite silently drops rows or shows broken views if YAML is malformed. Patrick + scripts must enforce strict templates.
Obsidian app UI lag: Heavy kanban + graph + Bases views on one big vault can stutter on Windows (reported FPS drops when scrolling large Bases); mobile is fine. Workaround: per-company sub-vaults or archived folders.
Search/index rebuild pain: With 2000+ files + attachments (photos of hotel rooms, signed PDFs) indexing slows slightly on cold start or after bulk auto-gen.
Git merge conflicts on auto-gen files: If two scripts regenerate the same .md or Bases cache at once.

Verdict for K1: CONDITIONAL GO. Perfect lightweight knowledge layer for AI context ingestion. Keep the “Patrick + scripts only” rule iron-clad and add YAML schema validation (e.g., via a simple n8n or Python pre-commit). At 5000+ files you would start feeling the pain — not yet.

2. K1+K2 dual-write risk (Second Brain & Email Drafter). What happens on drift? Which is source of truth?

This is the highest-risk part of the architecture — classic dual-write problem. Second Brain writes interaction notes to both Obsidian (rich Markdown context + links) and Supabase interactions table. Email Drafter reads both for context + deal history. If one write succeeds and the other fails, you get drift.

Named failure modes:

Partial write → stale AI context: Second Brain updates today.md but Supabase interactions fails (RLS, network, rate limit). Next @chatbot or Email Drafter reads old structured data → generic emails or hallucinated customer history.
GDPR / compliance ghost data: Obsidian retains deleted customer notes (human-readable) while Supabase purges them → audit nightmare in Finland.
Race conditions on high-volume days (peak booking season): Two staff trigger Second Brain simultaneously → duplicate or out-of-order entries.
Script drift over time: Auto-gen from K1 to K2 (or vice-versa) gets out of sync after version bump in n8n workflow.

Source of truth recommendation: Supabase (K2) is the single source of truth for operational data (customers, bookings, interactions, scores, logs). Obsidian K1 becomes the enriched, human/AI-readable view generated from K2 via one-way n8n scripts after every write. This eliminates bidirectional sync risk. Reverse (K1 → K2) is acceptable only for Patrick’s manual enrichment. Implement transactional outbox pattern in n8n or use Supabase realtime + Edge Function to trigger Markdown regeneration.

Verdict: High risk today, but fixable with clear SoT declaration + one-way sync. Without it the compound-interest promise collapses into data debt.

3. Single Supabase project with RLS per company_id — safe for 10 companies with different data sensitivities?

Yes, it is safe and the recommended pattern for your scale. Supabase (and Postgres) RLS is literally built for this: add company_id column everywhere, enable RLS on all tables, and write policies like:

SQL
Copy
CREATE POLICY "Users can only see their company"
ON interactions FOR ALL
USING (company_id = (SELECT company_id FROM profiles WHERE id = auth.uid()));

(or use JWT custom claims for tenant_id — very common). Thousands of multi-tenant apps run this way successfully.⁠Makerkit +1

Risks & failure modes:

Single RLS policy bug = full cross-company leak (e.g., missing company_id filter or auth.jwt() claim not set). One forgotten FOR ALL policy and every company can see everyone’s bookings.
Performance: RLS adds tiny overhead, but with proper indexes on company_id it is negligible at 2000 customers.
Backup / compliance: Finnish hospitality data sensitivities vary (VIP hotel guests vs. budget hostel). Single project means one backup contains everything — harder to prove isolation to DPO.

Separate Supabase projects per company? Overkill for 10 small entities under one holding. You would pay 10× compute, manage 10× connection strings, and lose easy cross-company analytics (your Power BI would need multi-source setup). Only do this if legal entities demand full physical isolation.

Recommendation: Stay with single project + RLS + automated policy tests (Supabase has great testing patterns). Add Row-Level Security audit via supabase audit or simple Edge Function logging. EU-Frankfurt location is GDPR-perfect.

Verdict for K2: GO (with mandatory RLS policy review + tests before go-live).

4. Truly compound-interest architecture or 4 separate systems creating overhead?

It is genuinely compound-interest by design — not four silos.

@scorer reads K2 scores → enriches K1 today.md → triggers K3 Power BI refresh → next AI feature sees richer context automatically.
Chatbot ingests tier-4 K1 → indexed in K2 → powers personalized replies using real booking history.
Every new AI feature (e.g., “upsell suggester”) can read the same enriched K1+K2 without new pipelines.
Git (K4) versions everything (prompts, n8n JSON, Power BI .pbix templates) so you can roll back a bad scorer change instantly.

This is exactly how the layers feed each other: unstructured knowledge makes structured data smarter, analytics surfaces it, Git keeps it auditable. Maintenance overhead exists but is low because:

Writes are restricted (Patrick + scripts).
n8n orchestrates most flows.
Power BI embeds are lightweight iframes and connect natively to Supabase Postgres (reliable for small/medium loads).⁠Draxlr

Remaining overhead risks:

Manual sync discipline between K1/K2.
Git merge conflicts on n8n JSON if multiple people edit workflows.
Power BI refresh latency if K3 is polled instead of using Supabase webhooks.

Verdict: Compound interest achieved. The architecture will get cheaper and smarter with every feature added, provided you lock in the SoT rule and RLS hygiene.

Final per-layer GO / CONDITIONAL GO / NO GO
K1 Obsidian Knowledge Layer: CONDITIONAL GO — scale is fine; enforce YAML + one-way sync from K2.
K2 Supabase Structured Layer: GO — production-ready with RLS discipline.
K3 Power BI Analytics Layer: GO — embeds work great; queries stay fast at this volume.
K4 Git Version/Audit Layer: GO — best-practice GitOps for prompts and n8n.

Next-step recommendations (immediate wins):

Declare Supabase as SoT and implement one-way K2→K1 regeneration script.
Add YAML schema validation + automated RLS policy tests.
Document the four-layer contract in the vault itself (meta!).

This setup is ready for production and will deliver the AI compounding effect you want. If you share the exact n8n sync flows or RLS policy examples I can stress-test them even deeper.
